_comment: The authoritative Compose runtime contract (issue #167, EPIC B #81 Phase 6).
Before this file the canonical compose definition was documentation-shaped:
its security posture was asserted in a comment, its field set was whatever
had accumulated, and an adapter agreeing with it was a matter of review. This
file is the contract-shaped version. It names every field the canonical
runtime definition must declare, and every host privilege the deployment must
not need, and distribution/compose's test suite fails the build when either
Two lists, deliberately asymmetric. `fields` is checked against the CANONICAL
definition only, because that is the artifact adapters derive from; holding a
derived artifact to the full field set would make it a second definition
rather than a derivation. `prohibited` is checked against the canonical
definition AND every derived artifact, because a prohibition an adapter can
opt out of is not a prohibition.
Roles, not service names. A service is the engine or the web UI because of
the command it runs, never because of what it is called: apps/truenas calls
them backup-manager/backup-manager-ui and the canonical file calls them
rclone-manager/web-ui, and a check keyed on the name would silently stop
checking the moment someone renamed one.
_derived_comment: Every artifact derived from the canonical definition. distribution/compose's
completeness guard fails when a compose file exists under apps/*/compose or
apps/*/catalog that is not listed here, so a new adapter cannot arrive
_dockge_comment: Dockge is not in the list above and has no entry of its own, on purpose
(issue #170). It deploys `canonical` itself, so it derives nothing: the
artifact the prohibition rules run over for Dockge IS the canonical
definition, already checked as the canonical definition. apps/dockge/ is
held to containing no runtime definition at all by
distribution/packaging's ScanForForkedStack, so this is an absence with a
check behind it rather than an omission.
_fields_comment: Every field carries a "derived" policy saying how it is checked on the
artifacts in "derived" above, because "the canonical definition declares it"
was never the same claim as "every adapter does". Five fields used to be
checked on NO adapter at all: CheckField only ever ran against the canonical
file, the derived artifacts went through the prohibition list only, and
derive.go covered seven fields that did not include timezone,
Four of the five converted platforms shipped without TZ as a result, on a
contract whose own reasoning is that retention's calendar boundaries depend
checked          CheckField runs against every derived artifact.
derivation-gate  distribution/packaging's derive.go checks it per adapter,
including the Unraid XML template this package cannot
canonical-only   deliberately not checked on derived artifacts, with the
reason stated in derivedWhy. This is the only way a field
may go unchecked, and it has to be typed on purpose.

fields.derivedWhy: distribution/packaging's derive.go checks it per adapter as image-reference, against canonical.json's one reference, and it reaches the Unraid XML template this package cannot parse at all.
fields.why: one canonical image, named identically by every service, so `command` is the only thing that varies between them.

fields.derivedWhy: derive.go checks it per adapter as runtime-profile: the command decides the role, and the profile has to be one canonical.json declares for that platform.
fields.why: the contract standardises 'command and runtime profile' as one field. A deployment that does not name its profile is a deployment whose host-dependent behaviour is implicit, which is the thing #167 exists to remove.

fields.derivedWhy: derive.go checks it per adapter as published-port, which is the stronger rule: exactly one published port in the whole adapter, on the Web UI, at the canonical listen port.
fields.why: the HTTP listen port, published by exactly one service. The engine deliberately declares none, which is why this field is required of the web UI role only.

fields.derivedWhy: derive.go checks it per adapter as health-check, across four metadata formats this package cannot parse. It has to be the derivation gate rather than a key-presence check here because the seams differ: the Web UI's check is a required override on every Compose adapter and a `--no-healthcheck` on Unraid, whose only seam is shell form the distroless image cannot run, and the engine's is a required declaration on every adapter that gates a start on it. Only a seam-aware rule can tell those apart.
fields.why: declared in the runtime definition rather than inherited from an image instruction and described in a comment. An operator reading this file has to be able to see what healthy means without reading the Dockerfile.

fields._derived_note: CHECKED on every derived artifact, not left to the derivation gate (issue #206). It used to be derivation-gate on the grounds that a derived artifact declares no engine healthcheck at all and inherits the image's, which canonical.json stated as the engine role's test - true while the image's instruction and the canonical engine check were the same command, and the whole of the defect once #167 made the canonical one a liveness probe and left the image's as the freshness verdict. Every derived Compose artifact now declares the start gate itself and is checked here, directly, in the file an operator reads. The derivation gate still checks it too, per adapter and across the four metadata formats this package cannot parse.
fields.why: the start gate has to be a liveness question, not a backup-freshness one. Every runtime definition's web UI declares depends_on: <engine>: condition: service_healthy, so whatever the engine's healthcheck asks is what stands between an operator and the only LAN-facing listener. `backup-manager status` exits non-zero on any DEGRADED, STALE or FAILING set and on a fresh install, which has backed nothing up yet and is legitimately not healthy, so gating on it means a stale backup set, or a fresh install, keeps the web UI from ever starting (issue #206). /health/live needs no configuration and is deliberately outside /api/v1. Backup freshness stays the operator and alerting surface it was built to be, and stays the image's own baked-in HEALTHCHECK for a plain `docker run`.

the declared grace period the runtime shuts down inside. Without it the value is Docker's own 10s default, which is a default rather than a contract, and nothing anywhere records what the application actually needs.
survive a crash and a NAS reboot, stay down when an operator stopped it on purpose.
explicit UID/GID rather than the image's build-time default, because the state directory's ownership is the host's business and not the image's.
a read-only root filesystem is what makes the writable paths explicit rather than implied.
retention is evaluated in a timezone. Leaving it to the image's UTC default means the calendar boundaries an operator reasons about and the ones the engine applies are silently different.

fields.derivedWhy: distribution/packaging checks every adapter's mounts, in whatever format they were written in: derive.go's storage-mounts rule for the container side and CheckStorageShapes for the write mode, both against canonical.json. It has to be there rather than here for two reasons. It reads each platform's own env file, so ${APPDATA:?...} and ${STATE_DIR:?...} resolve to the real host path instead of an unexpanded string this package would have to split on a colon that is inside a message; and it covers the Unraid XML template, which is not compose at all.
fields.why: the private application state: the lifecycle journal and the local-auth record. Separate from backup data, always. Writable, and said so rather than left to a default: the engine opens the SQLite journal for writing and creates its sidecar files, so a `:ro` here is a deployment that starts and then cannot record anything it does.

fields.why: the backup destination. Never the same mount as private state, and never a parent of it. Writable, and said so: this is the mount every retained artifact lands on, so a `:ro` here is a deployment whose backups silently do not happen, which is the worst failure this product has.

It has to be there rather than here for two reasons. It reads each platform's own env file, so ${APPDATA:?...} and ${STATE_DIR:?...} resolve to the real host path instead of an unexpanded string this package would have to split on a colon that is inside a message; and it covers the Unraid XML template, which is not compose at all.
fields.why: configuration comes from the host, never baked into the image, and the mount is a WRITABLE DIRECTORY the application owns rather than a read-only single file (issue #196). config.yaml lives inside it. The read-only single-file shape made three merged write paths inert inside a packaged container: every one of them replaces config.yaml through a temp file created in its own directory, which on that shape is the image's read-only rootfs. A directory can also be empty, which is how an app-store install honestly represents "not configured yet"; a bind mount cannot express that for a file, because Docker creates a directory at a missing source path.

fields.why: credential material is a read-only file mount and nothing else. No credential belongs in this file or in the environment.

fields.derivedWhy: an x-canonical-runtime document key. It states what the canonical runtime expects of a host, once. An adapter restating it would be a second answer that can be wrong on its own, which is what the derivation model exists to prevent.
fields.why: documented resource expectations, in the runtime definition rather than in prose that drifts from it.

fields.derivedWhy: derive.go checks it per adapter as supported-architectures: an adapter may make no architecture claim at all, and if it makes one it has to be the release's.
fields.why: the architectures this release claims. A deployment definition that does not say which architectures its image exists for cannot be checked against the release metadata.

fields.derivedWhy: an x-canonical-runtime document key. The digest policy belongs to the release, and an adapter that restated it could pin a different one.
fields.why: how an operator pins a release. A tag is mutable; the contract has to say what the immutable reference is and where it is recorded.

fields.derivedWhy: derive.go checks it per adapter as contract-version, through canonical.json's per-platform derivesFrom.contract, which is the mechanism that makes a contract change a visible edit in every adapter.
fields.why: the version of this contract the definition was written against, so a contract change is a visible edit rather than a silent divergence.

fields.derivedWhy: an x-canonical-runtime document key listing every profile that exists. An adapter selects one of them, which is checked as command-and-runtime-profile; restating the whole list would be a second registry.
fields.why: the profiles this runtime definition supports selecting, so `--profile=` above has a declared range rather than an open one.

_prohibited_comment: EPIC B #81 and issue #167's prohibition list. An absent setting and an
unnecessary setting are different claims, so these rules are only half the
evidence. The other half is a deployment that does real work without any of
them, and that already exists: apps/generic/tests/dockercli runs the real
built image with none of these settings, reaches health, and completes real
work. The static rules here prove the settings are absent; that suite proves
Each rule below has its own positive control in contract_test.go: the real
definition is mutated to require the setting, and the rule has to fire AND
name the service and the value. Three preflight rules in this repository have
already failed open, so a rule nobody has watched fail is a comment.

prohibited.why: privileged mode disables the container boundary entirely.
host networking puts the engine on every host interface, which is exactly the isolation the two-service topology exists to provide.
the host PID namespace lets the container see and signal host processes.
the host IPC namespace is shared memory with the host.
the Docker socket is root on the host with extra steps.
mounting a host system directory is unbounded host filesystem access; every path this runtime needs is a named mount.
least-privilege capabilities. Nothing this runtime does needs a capability a plain non-root process does not already have.
turning off the host's own confinement is the same class of exception as privileged mode.
